George
Be n s o n
From the very beginning,
the sound of the guitar
was always in my mind.
From the moment I heard
it, I knew that my life was
going to have something
to do with the guitar. I did
not know I was going to be
a player yet, but I loved the
sound.
                                    68
                           46




 As I grew older, I began to dabble with the guitar, to pick it up and try to pick things out. I would get so far, and
 then I would get stuck. I have found later that this is normal. Everybody goes through that on every instrument.
 To move forward, you have to take in more information, and look at things from different angles or from a dif-
 ferent point of view. So I started asking questions from the people whom I knew that had a certain mastery of the
 instrument.

 In my home town of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, a lot of traveling groups would come through town and I always went up
 to the guitar player to ask if he could show me something. I was never too ashamed to ask. The George Benson you
 know today is a collection of all those people who took the time to show me what they knew, and the things I could
 hang on to did me a lot of good.

 From guitar books, which I was not a reader, I was more of a picture guy. But the demonstrations in the new books
 really helped a lot to show the correct fingerings for this, that, and the other. They showed how to make chords.
 The chords led me to the harmony, that helped me to become a better single line player.

       Peter Farrell
                                  68
                           46




          Peter Farrell was born in Sao Paulo, Brazil in 1981. Son of the singer Claudia Fier and the
          saxophone player Lino Simão. He began studying music at school very young with an early
          interest in flute & violin.

          Still very young, his mother introduced him to the jazz and classical worlds, giving him the
          opportunity to hear the music of George Benson, Antonio Carlos Jobim, Debussy, Ravel,
          Bach, Dori Caymmi, Toninho Horta, Bill Evans, Herbie Hancock and many others.

          However, just like every teenager, Peter loved rock’n’roll and at the age of 11 he asked his
          mother to take him to a guitar teacher. So he began studying guitar with José Walter, which
          gave him the first basic steps to rock and blues.

                              2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
the George Benson Method                                                                                    4668




            One year later, the young boy was taken by his aunt Léa Freire and his uncle Sizão Mach-
            ado to a music conservatory called Groove, where he studied classical guitar, music
            theory, and jazz guitar with Leyve Miranda and Luis Cavalcante. In this period Peter
            started going deep into the music of George Benson and Wes Montgomery.

            Also in this period, Peter studied Brazilian music with the extraordinary guitar player Lula
            Galvão, and also piano with the great pianist and arranger Edmundo Cassis, who gave him
            a new vision about harmony.

            After many years of studying day and night, Peter started giving his first lessons and re-
            alized he had a great talent to teach and encourage others. Since then teaching has also
            become his passion.

            It did not take long until musicians all over the world started keeping their eyes on him
            because of his ability, technique and musicality. He was very advanced for an 18 year old
            boy. As a matter of fact, Peter was known in the musical scene as a prodigy since he was 14.

            Sometime later Peter was introduced to his idol and mentor George Benson. The connec-
            tion between them was instantaneous. The great Benson was amazed at Peter’s talent and
            how he had decoded many of his secrets. After a few months of friendship, Peter became
                                    68


            Mr. Benson’s private student and it has continued for the past 15 years.

            During the last six years Peter Farrell and George Benson have been dedicated to this col-
                           46




            lection of method books that they have created together: The George Benson Method.

            Peter Farrell has recorded and played with many great artists all over the world such as Jane
            Monheit, Brian McKnight, Eumir Deodato, Cesar Camargo Mariano, Romero Lubambo,
            Adam Rogers, and Didier Lockwood just to name a few.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.


George and I have been working for many years on this giant collection of books to give you the
best we can and help those that love the guitar the way we do. We hope this method can open a
                               68


new world that was unknown until now. You have a treasure in your hands. It contains all the
knowledge that George Benson has been teaching me privately over the last 15 years.
                      46




Thanks a lot,


Peter Farrell

help with the organization and visualization. Notice that depending on where and how we play
them on the fretboard, we will have more or less possibilities. Don’t let the time signatures
confuse you. Learn the ideas that you like the most and apply them where you feel they sound
the best. Give more attention to the single lines shown.

    George Benson’s Picking Technique
    For many years, guitar players all over the world have been trying to understand the George
    Benson right hand picking technique. However, different from what people may think and
    unfotunately have been teaching incorrectly, both hands must work together at all times,
    otherwise nothing is going to happen.

    So do not think that it is just a matter of copying the right hand position or even the angled way
    of holding the pick, because it will not work at all. Of course the angled pick is one of the most
    outstanding features of this technique, but let's understand that although it is important, there is
    no rule about how much the pick should be angled.

    The most important thing is to remember that there is no George Benson right hand technique
    without the left hand technique (fingering). The secret is the connection between both hands.
    And yes!.. we are talking about fingering and picking choices.

    It is disappointing to know that many guitar players around the world tend to give up on this
    technique thinking they are not good enough or don't have the talent to play this way. But do not
    worry, this method was created to help you and to show you all the secrets about using this
    technique that were not available until now.
                                   68


    Although the most important thing about this technique is the connection between both hands, in
    the beginning there are some right hand exercises that will help everyone to master and
    understand this technique correctly. In the following chapters, we will start connecting both
                          46




    hands using many different melodic ideas, phrases, scales and amazing licks inspired by George
    himself.

    Let’s start splitting the picking exercises into four types:

    1) Sweep Picking

    2) “Bee” Picking

    3) Rest Stroke Picking

    4) Jumping Strings

1                              2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
About the Left Hand Technique:
                                                                                                4668




In order to go deeper into the George Benson technique, we should learn some very
important facts concerning the left hand.


1) Correct Fingering (digital memory)
Play the exact suggested >ingering for each melodic line or example. They were chosen
speci>ically to better help you master this technique. Study the left hand >irst, and then
after you are comfortable with the left hand >ingerings, apply the right hand.

Sometimes, the type of >ingering George Benson uses can look dif>icult because he does not
use the pinky or 4th >inger very often, playing mostly with three >ingers. But as time goes
by, it will become easier and we will be able to play much faster and more articulate than
we had ever been able to play before.

Do not forget that our >ingers have digital memory, which means that they will learn what
we teach them. If our >ingerings are inconsistent, our >ingers will not learn anything and
they will always be lost. Now, what type of connection between both hands should we
expect if one of them is totally lost? Easy answer, none !!!
                             68


2) Drumstick Fingers
Let’s make our left hand work hard by hitting every note as if the >ingers were drumsticks.
                    46




A good exercise it is to play the following melodic line examples using only the left hand
before practicing with the right hand or connecting both hands. Note: Do not practice
anything without rhythm, and make sure every note is articulated.



3) Staccato
In order to play more rhythmic and precise, let's use a technique called staccato, which
means to mute all the notes with the left hand. In other words, we hit every note but we do
not depress the string all the way. Although it may seem very dif>icult to control in the
beginning, do not worry, the >irst step is to exaggerate the movement, thus teaching our left
hand >ingers to work together with the right hand picking.


                         2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                  2
    About the Number of Notes per String                                                         4668




    One of the most important things to correct the left hand 3ingering is the number of notes
    we play per string. The reason why it is so important is very simple: it can completely
    change the right hand picking, destroying the connection between both hands.

    A very important device concerning the "Bee" Picking Technique and the "Rest Stroke"
    Picking Technique, is that depending on the melodic line, the "down and up strokes"
    should be replaced by "up and down strokes", because everytime we want to change from
    one string to another, we should play an up stroke. So let's clarify with some examples
    below:

    1) Odd notes per string starting from the high and going to the low:
    In this case we should start with an up stroke independent from the rhythm used.
    However, be careful because some melodies might not work when rhythmically displaced.
    See below an example that works even when rhythmically displaced:

    Very Important:
    “Pull off” and "Hammer on” should be used with care, otherwise the articulation of our
    melodic lines can sound wrong or odd. Therefore, in the begining we should give priority
    to pick every note we play. However, later on we will understand their importance,
    especially when playing medium tempos.

“Bee” Technique
      68
 46




  2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   10
     The “bee picking technique" consists of fast "down & up strokes" which never lose contact                                  4668




     with the strings, only when changing from one to another. It is important to understand
     that this technique must be done using the wrist for medium tempos, and using the
     forearm for fast tempos. Usually it is easier to apply when we have chromatic ideas. See
     some exercises below:

Rest Stroke Technique
         68
    46




     2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   14

     the notes. It is quite similar to what gypsy guitar players do, alternating down and up

     this technique works together with the sweep technique. See some examples below:

“Jumping Strings”
   Technique
       68
  46




   2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   18
     The “Jumping String” technique, as the name suggests, is about playing notes on non                                                                                          4668




     consecutive strings. We play a determined note, and after that we jump one, two or even
     three strings to hit the next chosen note. This technique is one of the most difBicult to
     master, because we must keep using the wrist, and the hand will become tired easily. But
     nothing like practice everyday to get better.


     Below we have an exercise using the G major chord family containing many jumps between
     the notes. Notice that the pattern used for major 7th chords is different from the others,
     but only for a matter of taste.

Hammer on, Pull off
  & Slide Studies
        68
   46




    2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   20
     As mentioned before, hammer on, pull off and slide are some of the most important                                                                                             4668




     approaches for melodies when we play medium tempos. However, they can be extremely
     useful also in fast tempos to create different articulations, simulating a saxophone. It is
     extremely advisable that we sing everything we want to play or transcribe, before going to
     the instrument. After singing, try to transfer what you sing to the instrument, using
     everything you know (hammer on, pull off and slide), in order to @ind the best articulation.
     So as we can see, hammer on, pull off and slide are totally related with singing. Below we
     have some examples:

     Simple Chord Arpeggios
     Chord Arpeggio is a musical technique where we play notes from a determined chord one
     after the other. For harmonic instruments such as guitar and piano, we can use this type of
     technique in two different ways:
     a) MELODICALLY: When we play a chord arpeggio using single notes. We use this type of
        arpeggio for soloing.
     b) HARMONICALLY: When we play a chord arpeggio letting the notes ring into each other.
       We use this concept for comping, or solo guitar.
     Basically we have two types of arpeggio techniques, but let’s start with the simplest one:

     SIMPLE ARPEGGIOS: We use this technique over chords as the way they are presented
     (including inversions). This type of arpeggio works perfect with triads and their inversions,
     tetrads and their inversions, and extended chords in root position, because there are no
     inversions for extended chords. See the two examples below:


     1) Simple Triad Arpeggio:

                                                                                                       4668




                    Simple
                Triad Arpeggio
                   Exercises
                                     68


     The following exercises are very important to improve fretboard visualization, and also
     improve the way we approach triads on the instrument. Play the following exercises in four
     different ways:
                          46




     1) using the central shape
     2) using the right side shape
     3) using the left side shape
     4) mixing all the shapes the way you want to.


     Do not get discouraged if you cannot play the exercises fast or are unable to visualize all the
     possibilities. Choose the ones that you like the most, and later go back and explore the ones
     you left behind.

            Tetrad
      Fingering & Picking
          Possibilities
                                               Attention:


     All the following arpeggio examples are divided into two groups:

     a) Arpeggios with the root on the 5th string (key of “C”)
     b) Arpeggios with the root on the 6th string (key of “G”)
                                  68


     Each one of these groups will have three possibilities:
                         46




     a) left shape
     b) central shape
     c) right shape


     However, some examples had to be modiDied because it is not possible to play them in the
     determined keys. So we used the keys of “D” for the 5th string arpeggios and the key of “A”
     for the 6th string arpeggios.

     It is important to remember that, all the open strings (Dinger number “0”) can be replaced
     by the Dirst Dinger, when changing the key of the arpeggios. Note: Open strings were used
     on purpose in order to help us get used to replacing the open string with the Dirst Dinger.

         Simple Tetrad
           Arpeggio
           Exercises
                                         Attention:


The following exercises are very important to improve fretboard visualization, and also
improve the way we approach triads on the instrument. Play the following exercises in
                               68


four different ways:
                   46




1) using the central shape

2) using the right side shape

3) using the left side shape

4) mixing all the shapes the way you want to.



Do not get discouraged if you cannot play the exercises fast or are unable to visualize all
the possibilities. Choose the ones that you like the most, and later go back and explore
the ones you left behind.

 1st Inversion Triad
 Fingering & Picking
     Possibilities
                                         Attention:


The inverted arpeggios can be visualized many ways, depending on the guide root we
want to use (5th or 6th string). In many cases we can visualize the same arpeggio using
both guide roots. The following examples are just suggestions of how to approach
                           68


inverted possibilities.
                   46




The inverted arpeggio exercises are divided into two groups:
                      th
1) Arpeggios using a 5 string guide note (Key of “D”)
                      th
2) Arpeggios using a 6 string guide note (Key of “A”)

When possible, each one of these groups will have three possibilities:

a) left shape

b) central shape

c) right shape

                                                                                                  4668




              1st Inversion
                   Triad
                Exercises
The following exercises are very important to improve fretboard visualization, and also
improve the way we approach triads on the instrument. Play the following exercises in
four different ways:
                                68


1) using the central shape
2) using the right side shape
                     46




3) using the left side shape
4) mixing all the shapes the way you want to.


Do not get discouraged if you cannot play the exercises fast or are unable to visualize all the
possibilities. Choose the ones that you like the most, and later go back and explore the ones
you left behind. .


Note: There are no inversions for diminished or augmented chords, because they repeat
themselves in cycles. The diminished chord repeats itself every minor 3rd, and the
augmented chord every major 3rd. We call them: symmetrical chords. We will cover them
later on in more depth.

               2nd Inversion
                   Triad
                 Exercises
The following exercises are very important to improve fretboard visualization, and also
improve the way we approach triads on the instrument. Play the following exercises in four
different ways:


1) using the central shape
                                68


2) using the right side shape
3) using the left side shape
                     46




4) mixing all the shapes the way you want to.


Do not get discouraged if you cannot play the exercises fast or are unable to visualize all the
possibilities. Choose the ones that you like the most, and later go back and explore the ones
you left behind. .


Note: There are no inversions for diminished or augmented chords, because they repeat
themselves in cycles. The diminished chord repeats itself every minor 3rd, and the
augmented chord every major 3rd. We call them: symmetrical chords. We will cover them
later on in more depth.

Pentatonic Scale
The pentatonic scale has .ive notes as the name suggests (penta meaning .ive, therefore,
pentatonic means .ive notes). It is one of the most used scales in the music history. We
have 2 types of pentatonic scales:

1) "C" Major Pentatonic Scale:                             2) "C" Minor Pentatonic Scale
   (used for major chords)                                     (used for for minor chords)


 &                     w       w       w                    &w                         w   bw   w
     w     w    w                                                      bw          w
                 3     5        6       8                               b3         4   5   b7   8
       1   2                                                     1



The major pentatonic scale creates a major 6th chord (C, E, G, A), and the minor pentatonic
scale creates a minor 7th chord (A, C, E, G). So, for now we have the chords: C6 and Cm7.
However, if we change the key of the minor pentatonic from Cm to Am, we would have the
same scale and the same chord, because C6 is an inverted Am7 (1st inversion). See below:


"C" Major Pentatonic Scale (C6: C,E,G,A)            =      A Minor Pentatonic Scale (Am7: A,C,E,G)
                               68



 &w                    w       w       w                    &                              w    w
           w    w                                                       w          w   w
                                                                w
                     46




                 3     5        6       8                                              5   b7   8
       1   2                                                            b3         4
                                                                 1

With all that background, we could say that there is a relative major/minor relationship
between both pentatonic scales:

• C6       →     Am7 (relative minor chord of C6)

• Am7 →           C6 (relative major chord of Am7)

Although both pentatonic scales contain the same notes, it is extremely important to
visualize them separately (major and minor), because we will use them to split the guitar
fretboard into 5 zones. So depending where we are on the freatboard we will use one or the
other.

                           2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                    108

presented. This is not a rule. We could use the same chords we learned before, because they
are only to guide us into the 5 zones, nothing else.

Attention:
All the examples of pentatonic scales work perfectly when played vertically because they
can be played using two notes per string. However, we will learn other possibilities of how
to approach them over the guitar fretboard.

Although the pentatonic connections with alternate picking work perfectly when we use
the 1st or 6th string to change from one zone to another, we can also do this by using other
                                         68


strings if necessary. However, we must be careful because when we do this we must make
adjustments to preserve the connection between both hands.
                           46




For example:

If we are in the 1st zone going from low to high, and we want to move to another zone, we
must skip the 2nd zone thus going to the 3rd zone. This might look difGicult, but actually it
is much easier, otherwise the connection between both hands would be lost.

It is important to understand that among the many possibilities of Gingering and picking
we can Gind, we do not have to study all of them, only the ones we like the most, and feel
the most comfortable with.

Note: Do not pre judge the possibilities before you practice them. You may be surprised
when many things that in theory are not supposed to work well, work really well in
practice.

After learning the pentatonic scale, it is time to memorize some simple patterns using it.                                                                                                                                                                           4668




These patterns will help us to incorporate some melodic ideas. You can play them using
any rhythmic cell (even or odd). Although there is no rule about what the best way to use
these patterns are, there is a simple trick that works almost all the time, which is to
combine opposite ideas between melody and rhythmic cells. In other words, when the
melody is even, we use it over odd rhythmic cells, creating a very interesting effect. See the
example below of a 6 note pattern that will we will turn into a 16th note pattern:
Note: Remember that the order of the notes is always the same, the only thing that changes
is the rhythm, otherwise we would be changing the melodic pattern.

Notes:
This pattern is based on pull off and hammer on techniques, and it's a great oportunity to
learn new articulations and new connections between both hands. Notice that in these
exercises we have two types of picking patterns, one for the ascending movement and
                                             68


another for the descending movement, independent of zone.
In addition to using this pattern the way we have just shown, we can extend the melodic
                              46




concept by using the same pattern but changing from one key to another in the middle of
the line. It is a fantastic tool when we want to use some outside ideas. See a simple

                                             B b pentatonic
example below:

  1) This 6 note pattern idea was taken from George Benson's solo (3:15) in the song “ I’ll
                                      46




  Drink To That” from Jimmy Smith’s album “Off the Top”. It is a great exercise to practice the
  rest stroke picking technique. So be sure to play it correctly, remembering that everytime
  you use a down stroke it should rest on the next string.


  2) Some people believe that melodic patterns are not usefull to the language of improvisation
  because they are boring and predictable. As a matter of fact, they are not totally wrong.
  If we use them too much we will sound very predictable and not like creative improvisers.
  However, we should not be preoccupied with patterns or with any other melodic ideas,
  because it is just a matter of knowing when to use them. Actually the secret of a great
  improviser is to combine all the melodic ideas at once, creating a very interesting fusion
  between them.

Chapter 4

Blues – A First Step Toward Improvisation
No matter the style, everyone starts learning the blues to get into the world of
improvisation. The reason for this is because the blues basically has one scale (the blues
scale). It can be applied over all the chords in the blues form, including all the cadences and
turnarrounds. Later on we will learn how to use this scale over many types of songs.


The Blues Scale
The blues scale is a minor pentatonic scale with an added note. This note is called a "blue"
note. Normally we use this scale from the key we are in rather than over an individual
chord. Because it can be used over all the blues chords at once, this simpliBies playing over
all the chord changes. Be careful not to rely on this technique. It will make you sound like a
"lazy" improviser. Your lines will lack variation and will sound stagnant.

Because of the connection between the blues scale and the minor pentatonic scale we can
consider that there is a major blues scale, that actually will be the same scale, but
starting from the 3rd degree of the original blues scale (now minor blues scale). See below:
                                     68


1) "A" minor blues scale                             = 2) "C" major blues scale
                      46




                                                                                                  w    w
                                                          2

&                               w    w     w               & w         w bœ nw               w
    w     w    w #œ                  b7    P8                                                P5   M6   P8
               P4      #4       P5                                     M2      b3       M3
          b3                                                     R
    R
                       ↑                                                       ↑
                    Blue Note                                               Blue Note



However, what creates a bluesy sound is the combination of the minor blues scale with the
major blues scale in the same key. In other words, in the key of "C" for example, we would
have"C" minor blues scale working together with the "C" major blues scale.
Note: Blues scales played in the same key work only for major tonalities and not for minor,
where we use a “C” minor blues scale working together with “Eb” major blues scale.


                            2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                           140
  Summarizing:
                                                                                                  4668




  Minor Blues Scale
  The minor blues scale should be used over the major or minor tonality, summarizing all the
  chords from the major blues form or minor blues form. However, when mixed with the
  major blues scalein the same key, we can use it over any dominant 7th chord, bringing a
  blues vibe to it. (Make sure to play the major 3rd quickly in the phrase, otherwise the
  melody can sound wrong).



  Major Blues Scale
  The major blues scale can be played over any individual major chord, including the major
  7th and dominant 7th chords. However, this scale can sound not bluesy, so the trick is to
  mix it with the minor blues scale in the same key, reaching a bluesy sound and vibe.




  Play the Blues VS Play “ Bluesy”
  It is important to understand that we must study the blues form as a way to learn some
  extremely important musical concepts for improvising and also harmonizing. But actually
                               68


  there are two different ways of approaching it:
                       46




  a) Playing the Blues:
  We can play the blues (jazzy or not) with it's caracteristics: 12 bar form, blues scales, and
  lots of dominant 7th chords.



  b) Playing Bluesy:
  We can use some harmonic or melodic elements from the blues over other musical styles
  as well. For example, when we improvise over styles such Jazz, Soul, R&B and Pop Music,
  it is very common to use a blues phrase as a resolution of an idea. Harmonically, we can
  apply dominant 7th chords in uncommon places, when the melody allows.

  The advantage to playing horizontally (or laterally) is that we approach the guitar just like       4668




  the piano; when the melody needs to be high we go to the right, and when it needs to be
  low, we go to the left. Although it helps the brain to think more logically (words of Mr.
  Benson), sometimes there are exceptions, just like when we have to play opposite ideas in
  order to better connect the picking and Dingering.
  Note: Playing opposite ideas refers to inverting what we just stated about the piano.

Blues Scale Tricks
 for Major Blues
        68
   46




    2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   150
                                                                                                                                                                       4668




  Now that you know the blues scales, let’s learn some melodic “tricks”to use over the major
  blues form. Until now, what we knew is that both blues scales are the same, and that is
  totally true. However the way we are going to use them is going to be different.
  The ”tricky thing” in the major blues form is that we will not play both scales as being the
  same, we will use both in the same key, otherwise we would not have a new sound (color).
  See below:


  1) "C" major blues scale                                                               2) "C" minor blues scale


      &                                      ˙       ˙        ˙                          &˙                                                 ˙       b˙            ˙
          ˙        ˙ bœ           n˙                                                                   b˙                ˙ #œ
                         b3                  P5      M6       P8                                           b3            P4       #4    P5              b7        P8
          R        M2             M3                                                           R

  When we mix the major blues scale with the minor blues scale, we cannot summarize all
  the chords into one scale anymore, we must follow the harmony. In other words, the
  combination of both blues scales will work for each dominant 7th chord individually.
  Note: This will not work for minor blues form.


  Below we have two examples mixing the two blues scales (C7) :

Improvisation
 Positioning
      68
 46




  2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   154
                                                                                                     4668




  Improvisation is something that goes beyond our harmony knowledge and rhythmic concepts.
  First we must understand "when and how" this information is to be used to improve our solos. To
  make this clear, we will learn three ways to move our improvisation over song forms, and we will
  call this: improvisation positioning.



  1) Playing Early Notes:

  Improvise by playing early notes means to anticipate the melodies in anticipation of the chord,
  before the chord arrives. This is the most difficult positioning to master.



  2) Playing on the Head:

  Improvise by playing on the head means to follow the exact harmonies of the tune.



  3) Playing Late Notes:

  Improvise by playing late notes means to play after the chord changes. This is the easiest and
  simplest way.
                                68
                       46




  There are two different ways to use these three concepts above:



  a) You can play one scale, and what will be important is how you move rhythmically over the
  song. When we play a blues for example, we can use a simple pentatonic scale over the whole
  sequence of chords, we do not have to be concerned about which scales to use, only with
  positioning the melodies, even if they are simple.


  b) You can use these positioning concepts playing many scales but moving and following the
  harmony exactly. In other words, you change the scale when the harmony changes.


155                         2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Now that you know the three types of improvisation positioning, let's work with this concept          4668




using the major blues form. But before we start, it is important to understand that the blues is
divided into three parts that help us to improvise “telling a story” with a beginning, middle and
ending part. Next we have a chart that shows how we split the blues into three equal parts:
                                                                                         playing

                    C7                       F7                        C7

                    D7                       G7                 C7          A7    D7        G7

  Improving Your Blues Ideas
  Major Blues Licks
  Now that you have a basic understanding of how to play over the blues, let's learn some pre-set
  small musical ideas that we will call: “licks”. They are like words that we learn and
  memorize just like when we start speaking a language. In order to make this process easier,
  much more interesting and cooler, let’s play these licks over a rhythm called the boogaloo:

  (Note: A = bass drum E = snare )

      ? 44               œ.   œ œ œ œ             œ
             œ      œ
             TU     TU              DU PA DU
                         PA   PA                  PA

  • Below we have some George Benson songs using this type of rhythm:
  a) Footin't (Shape of Things to Come)                                  d) Giblet Gravy (Giblet Gravy)
  b) Bluesadelic (I got a Woman and Some Blues)                          e) Baby Workout (Big Boss Band)
  c) I Got A Woman (I got a Woman and Some Blues)                         f) Chiken Giblets (Benson Burner)

  Very Important:
  a) Sing the root of the chords from the blues form before start
                                       68


  b) Memorize these one by one, and never change before you have totally incorporated it into
     your playing.
                              46




  c) Do not forget to play the chords in the middle of the licks.
  d) Mix all licks and play them non stop.

  Blues form exercise guide:

 ⎮⎮44             F7          ⎮            B b7          ⎮               F7           ⎮       ‘          ⎮

 ⎮                B b7        ⎮            ‘              ⎮              F7           ⎮       ‘          ⎮

 Minor Blues Licks                                                                                   4668




 After learning some major blues licks, now it is time to learn some minor ideas that can be
 used over the minor blues. But be careful, because the minor blues form has two different
 types of chords (minor and dominant), so we must learn some substitution tricks before
 we start (Cm key):
 Attention:
 • Over A b7 play E bmi7 licks

 • Over G7 play A bmi7 licks

Notice that by doing this type of substitution, depending on the lick we might have some notes
that are not derived from the simple chords Ab7 or G7. But for now, it is not necessary to
understand the theory behind it, just memorize them.

So let's play them over the same groove we used for the major blues. See below:
(Note: A= bass drum      E= snare )

 ? 44               œ.    œ œ œ œ            œ
        œ       œ
        TU     TU              DU PA DU
                    PA   PA                 PA



 Just like the major blues "small licks", the following exercises will help you to understand how
                                  68


 to incorporate the concept "playing early notes" anticipating the melodies of the next chord.

   Extended Blues Licks
                                      Attention:

Next, we have many examples of extended blues licks in the key of “C”. It is important to
understand that in theory, we could use all of them over any major or minor chord, because
we are talking about the blues.


However, when the melodic line is built from the minor pentatonic scale without any
mixture of the major pentatonic scale, our preference is to use the lines over minor chords
or chord sequences belonging to the "minor chord family" (natural minor harmonic Eield).


This is not a rule. Melodic lines using only the minor pentatonic scale will often work
perfectly over major chords such as C6, Cmaj7 and of course C7. In addition to this, we can
also apply these lines over chord sequences belonging to the "major key chord family"
                             68


(natural major harmonic Eield).
                    46




In the begining of each melodic line we have given some chord possibilities that these lines
will work over. Remember that blues lines work differently than other types of lines, as
they can be played in many different harmonic situations.


The secret to mastering when and where to use these melodic lines is quite simple: learn to
sing every melodic line (lick) that you know. Internalize the sound. If you do this, as time
goes by things will become easier and you will know exactly when and where to use them.


Note: When studing the melodic lines, never forget the importance of connecting both
hands. So follow the given Eingering & picking possibilities exactly as notated for each one
of the examples.

      Double Stop Licks
             68
        46




235      2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
In the next exercises let’s split the possibilities of double stops using two guiding roots: one
                                                                                                   4668




on the 5th string and another on the 6th string. It is important to understand that this type
of tool (double stops) can be used over any dominant 7th chord to create a blues vibe.

But let’s remember that we can use every blues idea over major 6th or major 7th chords,
creating a blues vibe. Therefore, in theory the following melodic examples can be used
over the chords: C7(including all the alterations), C6 and Cmaj7 (including Am7).

However, in minor keys we must be very careful about what type of blues double stops we
use. Actually we have two speciHic situations. Let's use "Cm" as an example:

a) Static minor chords (Am):

We can use the blues double stops derived from “C” (which is a combination of “C” major
pentatonic with “A” minor pentatonic). Also we can use double stops derived from "A" minor
pentatonic adding the major 6th.

b) Over progressions in minor keys such IIø, V7, Im (in the key of Am : Bø, E7, Am7)

In this case we should use only the double stops derived from “A” minor pentatonic or “C”
major pentatonic which are the same thing (Am = C).

Although we have all these chord possibilities, we should never forget that blues ideas must
be used mainly in the key of the song, so we must always pay attention to the harmony to
understand what to play. See some examples below:
                              68


1) || Cmaj7 | Bbmaj7 ||
                     46




• play double stop ideas in the key of “C” (always end the melodies on a chord tone).


2) || Abmaj7 | Gsus | Cmaj7 | C6 ||

• play double stop ideas in the key of “C” always end the melodies on a chord tone. Be
careful to not play the major 3rd ("E" natural) of "C" over the Abmaj7 chord.


3) || C7(13) |     %    | Ab7(13) |          %     ||

• play double stop ideas in the key of “C” over C7 and in the key of “Ab” over Ab7(13).




                          2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                236
                                                                                                   4668




  4) || Cm7 | Ab7(13) ||

  • play double stop ideas in the key of “Eb” over Cm7 (excluding melodies derived from
  “Ebm” ) and play double stop ideas in the key of “Ab” over Ab7(13).



  5) || Fmaj7 |       Em7 | Dm7 | Am7 ||

  • play double stop ideas in the key of “C” .



  6) || Cm7(9) | Dø G7(b13) ||

  • play double stop ideas in the key of “Cm” or “Eb”, excluding melodies derived from “Eb”
  minor pentatonic.


  7) || C7(13) | F7(9) ||

  • play double stop ideas in the key of “C”. Be careful to not play the major 3rd ("E" natural)
  of "C" over the F7 chord.
                                68


  8) || Fmaj7 | Bb7(9) | Cmaj7 | C6 ||
                       46




  • play double stop ideas in the key of “C”.


  9) || Am7 | D7(9) ||

  • play double stop ideas in the key of “C” and also Am pentatonic including the the major
  6th.


  10) || Cm7(11) | Bbm7(11) ||

  • play double stop ideas in the key of “Cm” or “Eb”.

Natural Major Scale Application
As we have learned, the natural harmonic scale, also known as the Ionian Mode, is the
mother of six other scales and together they form the seven harmonic ;ield modes. We will
concentrate on the two related modes, Ionian and Aeolian. We will summarize the seven
scales of the harmonic ;ields into these two scales.

We can improvise over any chord or any sequence of chords belonging to any harmonic
;ield simply by using the Ionian or Aeolian Mode of the key we are in. We call this approach
"key improvising" or "key improvisation". We will go deeper into the other modes later in
our studies. For now, we will create the sounds of all the modes using the Ionian and
Aeolian scales.



Attention:

Be careful with the avoid notes of both scales (perfect 4th in the Ionian mode, and ;lat 6th
in the Aeolian mode), because they can clash with the melody note, when played over the
                              68


key or relative chord. In the key of “C”, the avoid note will be “F”, which should not be used
over Cmaj7 or Am7. But remember that there are always exceptions and at times the avoid
note works ;ine depending on the situation.
                     46




So in the beginning we will learn simple melodic patterns that will help us get familiar with both
scales, DO NOT rely on these. Remember these are only exercises and can sound very predictable.
This is the first step on the long road that we have ahead of us.

Note: As the following pattern exercises were built using “C” Ionian and “A” Aeolian, they
can also be played over any chord or sequence belonging to “C” Natural Major Harmonic
Field or “A” Natural Minor Harmonic Field.

Before learning some of these patterns for the Ionian and Aeolian Modes, let’s learn some
important approach techniques concerning the visualization of the guitar fretboard.




                          2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                 244
                                                                 4668




       The 5 Vertical
      Major Scale Zones
             68
        46




245      2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Ionian & Aeolian
                                                                                                                4668




One of the most dif-icult things for guitar player, is to master the scales and other melodic
ideas all over the guitar fretboard. The reason for this is because the fingerings constantly
change from one position to another. So in order to solve this problem, let’s split the fretboard
into -ive vertical zones. It is important to understand that the vertical visualization is the
key to playing horizontally, because it makes it possible to connect the fretboard zones
going from one to another without getting lost. In other words, we visualize vertically but
play horizontally most of the time.



Let’s start visualizing the Ionian and Aeolian scale (key & relative scale) in the five vertical
zones. Each zone will be related with a chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7). The chords will guide
us better then just single notes, because they are -ixed structures, which are easier to
remember rather than a lot of single notes. Make sure to use the root of each chord to
guide you in each zone.

exceptions, and sometimes both work perfectly. Next we have many examples of Ionian and
Aeolian scales vertically and horizontally. Choose the examples you like the most, memorize
them and have fun.

Intervallic Patterns
         68
    46




     2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved   252
  Rhythmic Exercises Using Intervallic Patterns                                                     4668




  In the beginning we will learn some simple intervallic patterns that will help us get familiar
  with the two scales we have just visualized all over the guitar neck. But DO NOT rely on
  these. They are exercises and can begin to sound very predictable and extremely boring.

  However, we can make them sound better when we use them applying some rhythmic
  tricks. Next we have some rhythmic "motifs" forming what we call "rhythmic displacement".
  Every intervallic pattern should be applied using them. In order to make some patterns
  sound more musical, we can start every motif repeating the last note of the previous motif.
  (this usually works better with three note rhythmic motifs). See the examples below:
  • Walking in 3rd's:
  C, E, D, F, E, G, F, A and so on…
  Note: We have a very special rhythm book for those that want to go deeper into studying the
  concept of rhythmic displacement, and also many other studies about rhythm.

  Chapter 7
                                                                                                  4668




  The Secret of the Two Chords
  As mentioned before, the natural major scale is one of the 5irst subjects we must study to
  start improvising. It can summarize the whole harmonic 5ield into one scale. However, the
  avoid note (perfect 4th) can create some melodic problems, especially over the root chord
  and the relative minor chord (Cmaj7 and Am7 in the key of “C”).

  However this scale works perfectly when played over Dm7 (Dorian), Em7 (Phrygian), Fmaj7
  (Lydian), G7 (mixolydian), Bø (locrian), even while using the avoid note. We must be
  careful with our note choices. For example over a G7 chord, we should not stop on a "C"
  note. The only exception for this would be when we have a Gsus7 chord, because in this
  case the “C” is a chord tone and it will work perfectly.

  But for now, let’s concentrate on two chords: Cmaj7 and Am7, ignoring for a moment the
  rest of the chords from the harmonic 5ield. In order to solve the avoid note issue, we will
  not use it for the time being. Therefore, we will create melodies for Cmaj7 that can 5it over
  Ionian or Lydian chords, and melodies for Am7 that can 5it over Dorian or Aeolian chords.
  This is the beginning of what we will call “The Secret of the 2 Chords”.
                               68


  As mentioned before, it is not enough to only use the scales of the chords to create
  melodies, we must add stronger melodic structures to them such as triads and tetrads . As
  we will not be using the avoid note (F) over Cmaj7 and Am7, we will discard all the triads
                      46




  and tetrads that contain an "F" note (4th degree). See the remaining chords below:


  • Tetrads: Cmaj7, Em7, Am7

  • Triads: C, Em, G, Am


  I bet you are asking yourself what about the other chords of the harmonic 5ield, how can
  we just forget them? Later on, we will use the major 7 lines and minor 7th lines over other
  chords, creating the sound of the modes without thinking about them, just like we did
  using the harmonic 5ield chords over a continuous bass note. But for now let’s focus in
  “Major 7th and Minor 7th chords”.

  • For Am7 we will add: major 2nd and perfect 4th;

                                           2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                 272
  Chord Superimposition (Chord Stacking)
                                                                                                 4668




  The word superimpose means to join, add, propose an idea or concept based on another
  existing idea. In music, it means using more than one chord simultaneously in a melodic or
  harmonic form. Harmonically, it is the joining of two or more chords forming a single chord.
  Melodically it is to play notes from two or more different chords over a determined chord.
  The superimposition is a simpler and more melodic way of using the notes of a scale,
  without thinking of them as single notes, but as part of a pre established melodic structure
  such as triades and tetrads. John Coltrane used to call this: “chord stacking".
  It is important to understand that superimposed chords or stacking chords only works
  using triads and tetrads for a simple reason, the tensions are created by the mixture of two
  or more chords, so there is no need to use extended possibilities.




  “Chord Stacking” Examples:
  If we play Gmaj7 (G, B, D, F# ) over the Cmaj7, we would have a “C “ Lydian sound
  melodically, and a Lydian chord harmonically. However it is difHicult to play these
  superimposed chords correctly on the guitar. The only instrument that can apply this
  harmonic concept correctly is the piano. To achieve this on the guitar, we must arpeggiate
  two chords, one after the other, forming one chord. We call these: "block chords".
  The best way to understand the superimposed chords is through chord arpeggios.
                                68


  See below:
                       46




  Example 1:
  if we have a Cmaj7(9) arpeggio, we will have:

  C, E, G, B, D

  |-------| = C major triad (C, E, G)
      |----------| = Em7 tetrad (E, G, B, D)
        |-------| = G major triad (G, B, D)


273                         2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Example 2:                                                                               4668




if we have a Dm7(9)11 arpeggio, we will have:

D, F, A, C, E, G

|----------| = Dm7 tetrad (D, F, A, C)
  |----------| = Fmaj7 tetrad (F, A, C, E)
     |-----------| = Am7 tetrad (A, C, E, G)
        |-------| = C major triad (C, E, G)




More Examples:
1) C + G = Cmaj7 (9)                   5) C + D = Cmaj7 (#4)

2) C + E = Cmaj7 (#5)                   6) C + F# = C7 (b9, #11)

3) C + Em = Cmaj7                       7) C + Gm = C7(9)
                            68


4) C + Edim = C7                        8) Cm + Db = C Phrygian
                    46




We can also stack two or three chords and choose another bass note that does not have
any connection to them. See the examples below:


1) Bb + F over C = C7sus(13)

2) Eb + Bb over C = Cm7(9, 11)

3) Eb + F over C = Cm7(6)

4) C + F# + A = C7(b9, #11, 13)

5) F# + G# = C7(b9, #9, #11, b13)


                        2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved           274
  After learning the scale arpeggios, it is time to learn a new melodic approach, which                                                                                              4668




  consists of some superimposed chord arpeggio possibilities, that can be played over Cmaj7
  and Am7. Notice that the ascending arpeggios will de;ine the fretbord zones, because the
  descending arpeggios will almost always use two zones, because we play descending
  arpeggios vertically. Note: None of these examples contain avoid notes.
  The examples on the following pages, where we have many possibilities of arpeggios over
  the ;ive fretboard zones, ARE NOT MELODIC LINES to be memorized and played one after
  another, each arppeggio is an example of what we can use in every zone with the correct
  picking & ;ingering. Later on, on the following pages we will have melodic lines to
  memorize, helping us to understand how all these arpeggios will work together.

How do we start speaking ?
Although melodic lines", also known as “licks" or simply “single lines”, are one of the most
important studies in learning the language of improvisation, they must be studied carefully
and correctly, as they can help or sti=le the creative process.

Many people do not believe that memorizing melodic lines is helpful when learning how to
improvise, as they argue that students should create their own ideas rather than copy
from others. However, let's change the musical focus and use another subject to make this
clear.

We all learn to speak by repeating and copying the words we hear from those around us.
Can you imagine how many times a day a child repeats the same words in order to
incorporate and learn them? Or even, can you imagine how many times a day an adult
speaks the same words, in different situations, with another connotation and in different
order ? Well ... the answer for both will be thousands of times.

Music is exactly like a language, if we want to learn it, we must know the words, the
phrases, the intonations and so on. So, the best way to learn is to listen and copy from the
greatest artists we love, until we develope our own way to communicate, combining
everything we know.
                              68


It is important to understand that we must learn to sing melodies of songs and solos of
our favorite artists. It does not matter what the style is. The following melodic lines (licks)
are just a musical way to learn how to improvise, how to better visualize the guitar neck
                     46




and how to improve our technique.

The purpose of this book is not just proving the importance of memorizing many licks. It
is to show how to understand, organize and "transcend" what we transcribe =inding out
the musical concepts behind them. For example, a simple "lick" can teach us a complete
harmonic concept, allowing us to create countless new lines from it.

Do not skip any chapter, because they are connected and need each other to be completely
understood. It is very important to always be studying GBI 1 and 2, because through them
we will incorporate the necessary rhythmic vocabulary so that, over time, we can change
the rhythm of the lines appropriately and with good taste.



                          2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved               280
  How to Organize and Learn Single Lines
                                                                                                  4668




  Like grammar, melodies are also organized into words, phrases, sentences, paragraphs, and
  so on. A melodic line can have several words, forming several phrases, which, for example
  can form a sentence. There is no rule regarding the length of the line, but for now we will
  consider one bar for each melodic line. However, the line can begin in the last beat of the
  previous bar or even resolve on the ?irst beat of the next bar.

  It is very important to understand the small movements that form a line. In other words,
  we must know how each line was built, how many "words" or "phrases" it has, in order
  to know where to break it when we need to link it to another line. The separation of words
  of a melodic line must be done carefully. In theory ever small movement should always
  end on a note of the chord, with some exceptions. As time goes by, things will become
  clearer.

  In the beginning, do not worry about playing all the melodic lines you have memorized in
  all the keys. Play them in the same key for a while, trying to learn new possibilities on the
  higher and lower strings. Then, when you feel comfortable, practice in a different key
  everyday (Do not worry we will have a lot of examples showing how to study).

  Consider this book as a "guide" of possibilities, almost a dictionary of licks that we use
  from time to time to guide us. Below we have an example of how we should divide a line:

  a) Word (4 sixteen notes)
                               68



      & œ œ œ œ
                      46




  b) Phrase (at least union between two words)

      & œ œ œ œ œ bœ œ #œ

  c) Sentence (at least union between two phrases)
                                 œ œ #œ œ œ
                œ b œ œ #œ œ œ œ                                                   w
      & œ œ œ œ

Octave Displacement                                                                                                4668




Octave displacement is a musical term that describes the changing of direction of a scale
line, in other words, it describes when a scale line changes to a diffent octave. This
technique has been used since the Renaissance Period, more precisely in Baroque with the
use of COUNTERPOINT.

But to clarify the idea let’s understand what counterpoint is. In music, this term refers to
a compositional technique in which the melodies are harmonically independent but have a
relationship between each other. The starting point for counterpoint is the creation of a
Eixed melody or main voice that we call CANTUS FIRMUS. The next step is the creation of
melodies that will be the harmony part of the cantus formus.

There are many types of counterpoint with many different rules, and that will lead us to
what we call species counterpoint, a method that has been the basis for polyphonic music.
Each species of counterpoint has different rules and the melodies must follow them in
relation to the cantus Eirmus.

So, among many techniques of how to create melodies with a harmonic relationship
between each other, the octave displacement is one of the most useful, and it may help the
composer to follow the rules and Eind better solutions for each counterpoint species.
However, we can use this technique when we have a single melody, such as the example
below taken from Sonata I for Violin (presto).

                                               A, G, F # , E, D, C   B b, A, G, F, E, D   C # , B b, A, G, F, E
                             68


(J.S.Bach)                                    ↓--------------↓ ↓--------------↓           ↓---------------↓
                                                                       œ          œ œ œ œ nœ
&    bb   œ œ œ œ œ œ                œ                          œ œ œœ   n œ œ #œ
                        œ œ œ œ œ œ œ #œ nœ œ
                    46




                                                   cresc.



                                             * Notice that in the example above, J. S. Bach used
                                             consecutive scale notes with octave displacement


The technique of octave displacement is also found in bebop as well. If we analyse the solos
or even the themes composed by Chalie Parker, Bud Powell, Dizzie Gilespie and many other
bebop players, we will see that it’s a very common occurence, but more than that, it is a
very usefull technique that gives more melodic possibilities to the same single line idea.
Let’s see some examples on the next page:

Changing the Rhythm of your Single Lines                                                                         4668




The melodic lines on the following pages are presented using mostly sixteen notes on
purpose, as the focus is learning melodies. However, it is necessary to know some rhythmic
tricks, in order to play them differently each time, otherwise we could not develop our
improvisation concept.
We can use these rhythmic substitutions on any beat in the bar, but the rhythmic
replacement cell must have the same number of notes as the original cell. When needed,
we can add one or two extra notes to the phrase to improve the quality of the melody, or
even to be able to create a non-predictable phrase.
It's important to understand that some possibilities may not work well, but in order to know
which one is the best we should test all of them. As time goes by, we will be much more
comfortable about using different rhythms while playing "licks". See some possibilities:

  Applying Inverted Triad Arpeggios                                                                                                                     4668




  It is important to remember that we can also use inverted chords to build melodic lines.
  In theory all the inverted chords that we have used in this chapter would sound great.
  However inverted triads tend to sound better than inverted tetrads, because they are
  stronger melodic structures. But we must remember that tetrads can also sound beautiful
  in many cases. Below we have a table of inverted triad possibilities for each fretboard zone.

  Attention:
  Notice that sometimes triads require the use of the complete sweeping technique, that
  means going up and down keeping the same @luency and consistency. The following
  examples are not melodic lines to be memorized, they are only examples of what we can
  add to build melodic lines.

Before continuing on with more melodic line examples, this time adding the 2nd inversion triads,
let's be clear why we are not using inverted tetrads. First of all, it is important to understand that
some intervals are "stronger than others". The strongest intervals are a 3rd, 4th and 5th. This is
the reason why the strongest chord construction we have in western harmony are:


1) Tertian Chords: built from superimposed 3rds;

2) Quartal Chords: built from superimposed 4ths.




                                                   2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                                                                       300
  Maybe you are asking yourself: Why are we excluding tetrads if most of them are tertian
                                                                                                                                                  4668




  chords? To quickly answer this question let's look at what happens when we invert triads
  and tetrads:

  Triad Inversions: (key of “C”)

                                                                                                                          3rd
                                                                                                                                        œ
                                                                                                            4th
      &                                œ                                  œ           œ             œ                 œ
          œ              œ                                œ
                                 3rd                            3rd            4th
                3rd

  Tetrad Inversions: (key of “C”)


                                                                                                                                              œ
                                                                                                  3rd                         3rd       3rd
                                                                                    3rd 2nd
                                                                                                        œ                           œ
                                                                                                                  2nd
      &œ                     œ     œ                  œ         œ         œ    œ       œ      œ                   œ       œ
                    œ                       œ
                                                                    2nd
              3rd       3rd 3rd                 3rd       3rd


  Notice that when we invert triads they always use the stronger intervals, 3rds and 4ths.
  However, when we invert tetrads they also create the interval of a 2nd, which is a weaker
  interval.

  In addition to tetrads, the same "problem" occurs with quartal triads because it's root
                                                68


  position and 1st inversion contain an interval of a 2nd, leaving only it's third inversion
  with the strongest intervals.
                                   46




  Quartal Triad Inversions: (key of “C”)
                                                                                                                          4th
                                                                                      œ
                                                                                                        4th
                                                                                                                      œ             œ
      &œ                 œ             œ                  œ               œ                        œ
                                 2nd                            2nd           4th
                4th


  Summarizing, tetrads are melodically strong only when played in the root position, and
  quartal triads in the 3rd inversion. This is not a rule, it is a suggestion that will help you to
  build better and beautiful melodies.

307                                                            2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Applying Quartal Melodic Ideas                                                                                                                                      4668




The quartal melodic ideas are melodies using consecutive 4ths, forming many "sus chords".
This type of approach is very important not only to create melodies, but for harmony.
However, in this book we will cover only some melodic examples that will be connected
with the scale arpeggios and also common arpeggios.

It is important to mention that we will not use quartal ideas containing the major scale
avoid note 4th, just like we did with arpeggios and scale arpeggios. Therefore, we can
have the possibilities below to build our melodies:

1) D, G, C                       3) A, D, G

2) E, A , D                      4) B, E, A

Note: We will study the inverted quartal triads later in the next GBI Books. For now,
enjoy the melodies formed by consecutive 4ths (Quartal Triad 3rd Inversion).

      Using Cmaj7 Ideas
      over Other Chords
              68
         46




317       2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
Now that we understand that we consider Cmaj7 and Am7 the same chord, every time we           4668




see a Cmaj7 chord we can interchange it with an Am7 chord. So now let's understand how
to apply the "secret of two chords" over other chords.
Let’s take Dm7 dorian as an example. First of all, let's understand that if we consider a
chord as being dorian, it means that it is the IInd degree of a determined harmonic Cield,
which can be hidden or not (in the case of Dm7 dorian the key is "C"). But it is very
important to understand that any mode can be used over any chord. When we refer to the
dorian mode as the IInd degree of a determined key, we are saying that there is a chord
family that can be played on that chord, independent from the harmonic situation it is
placed. (in other words a dorian chord does not have to be the IInd degree of the key of a
song, but it is the IInd degree of the key it creates).
Therefore, if Dm7 dorian creates the "C" major chord family ("C" natural major harmonic
Cield) , it means that we can apply all the melodic material of Cmaj7 & Am7 over Dm7,
including arpeggios and scale arpeggios.
By doing this we can Cind beautiful melodies to a dorian chord. However, as we are not
using the avoid note "F" in the Cmaj7 & Am7 ideas, the Dm7 dorian chord would be
incomplete because "F" is the 3rd , which being a common note for this chord is
necessary. So in order to solve this problem , we must transpose the same ideas of
Cmaj7 & Am7 into Dm7 & Fmaj7, now having 4 different chords to play over Dm7 dorian.
The secret is to combine these 4 chords making them sound as one, Dm7 dorian. Later on
we will have many examples of how to do this. The same process can be done with other
modes. See Below


Creating the sound of all the modes using “Chord Stacking”
                            68


Below we have some options of how to apply “The Secret of the Two Chords” over all the
harmonic Cield chords, which will help us create the sound of each individual mode.
                   46




Note: Pay attention to the ending note, it can make your melody sound good or wrong.


• Cmaj7 Ionian: play Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7, Dm7
• Dm7 Dorian: play Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7, Dm7
• Esus(b9) Phrygian: play Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7, Dm7
• Fmaj7 Lydian: play Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7, Dm7
• G7 Mixolidyan: play Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7, Dm7
• Am7 Aeolian: play Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7, Dm7
• Bø Locrian: play Cmaj7, Am7, Fmaj7 , Dm

                        2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved                318
  Creating “Out Side Ideas”                                                                       4668




  It is important to emphasize again, that the “secret of the two chords” is based on major 7th
  and minor 7th chord arpeggio ideas using some added notes, not scales. Therefore, in order
  to make it work, we must memorize some melodic lines, that as time goes by will be
  transformed and played differently every time we use them.
  In addition to creating the sound of the modes without playing scales, we can also use
  major 7th and minor 7th chord arpeggio ideas to create substitute harmonies, resulting in
  what we call “out side melodies”. When we do this, we add notes that do not belong to the
  preset harmony, but they work well because they create different colors over the chords,
  making the melodies become hybrid, and not predictable as lines that use one concept or a
  scale wise approach.
  In order to go deeper into the concept of the “secret of the two chords”, let’s learn how to
  apply it over dominant 7th chords that have the function of leading to other chords. Let’s
  use the altered chord as an example, because it has all the tension notes we need. We have
  Eive speciEic cases. (C#7alt chord as example below):

  • C#7alt → As we know an altered chord can be:
  a) C#7(#9)      b) C#7(b9)           c) C#7(#11)           d) C#7(b13)


  Attention:
  It is important to understand that this concept can be used over a static altered chord, or
                               68


  over any dominant 7th chord that has the function of leading to other chords. For example,
   we could use it over a C#7(b9)13 leading to F#maj7, or over a C#sus(b9) leading to F#m7 ,
  even knowing that these chords do not belong to the altered chord family.
                      46




  Case 1: Major 7th Chord a 3rd above the Altered Chord
           Minor 7th Chord half step above the Altered Chord
           (Fmaj7 & Dm7 over C#7alt)

  Through the tritone substitution, we know that C#7 is the same chord as G7. However, if
  we consider the G7 as a mixolydian chord, it will lead us to Dm7 dorian (they work together
  in the IIm/V progressions). But let’s forget scales for a while and think only about chords
  and “pure” melodic lines. In addition to the connection between Dm7, G7 and C#7, we have
  one more chord, the Fmaj7, which is the relative major of Dm7. So, to improvise over a
  C#7alt chord, we can use Dm7 and Fmaj7 “pure” melodic lines. Note: “pure” means no
  avoid notes.


319                        2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved
                                                                                                4668




                  th
Case 2: Major 7 Chord half step below the the Altered Chord
         Minor 7th Chord half step above the Altered Chord
         (Cmaj7 & Am7 over C#7alt)

As we have just learned in case 1, we can use Dm7 and Fmaj7 melodic lines over C#7 altered
chord. But if we consider the Dm7 chord as dorian the hidden harmonic 9ield will be “C”
major, which give us Cmaj7 and Am7 as the root and relative chords. In other words, over
a C#7 altered chord, we can also use Cmaj7 and Am7 “pure” melodic lines.




Case 3: Major 7th chord 1 and a half step below the Altered Chord
         Minor 7th Chord a tritone above or below the Altered Chord
        (Bbmaj7 & Gm7 over C#7alt)

Case 3, was taken from some bebop turnaround ideas. But this one in particular we will call:
chromatic turnaround. The bebop musicians used to change the turnaround cadence from:
I, VI7, IIm7, V7 into IIIm7, bIIIm7, IIm7, V7. So, if we consider the C#7 as the VI7 we would
have the cadence: Emaj7, C#7, F#m7, B7. Now, let’s apply the substitution: G#m7, Gm7,
F#7, B7. Based on this, we can use Gm7 “pure” melodic lines over C#7alt chord. Of course
we cannot forget that Gm7 has a relative major, which can also be used over C#7alt: Bbmaj7
                              68
                       46




Case 4: Major 7th a tritone above or below the Altered Chord
         Minor 7th Chord a minor 3rd above the Altered Chord
        (Gmaj7 & Em7 over C#7alt)

This case is based on the fact that we can change the characteristics of any chord by using
the modal interchange concept. If we consider the C#7alt as a C#sus(b9), in other words a
Phrygian chord, we will 9ind a Gmaj7 chord, which is the same chord with a different bass
note. After 9inding the Gmaj7, we can 9ind Em7 (relative of "G"). In other words, we can use
Gmaj7 and Em7 melodic lines over C#alt chord.




                          2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ltd. All Rights Reserved            320
                                                                                                 4668




                   th
  Case 5: Major 7 half step above the the Altered Chord
           Minor 7th Chord whole step below the Altered Chord
          (Dmaj7 & Bm7 over C#7alt)

  Although this case is not so common, it is based on the fact that we can replace V7, by
  IIø/V7. In other words, we can substitute C#7alt for the cadence G#ø, C#7alt . However, as
  we have learned previously in the Harmonic Region chapter, the IIø can be replaced by
  the IVm, which also leads us to bVImaj7 (relative chord from the IVm). This type of approach
  makes the dominant 7th chord sound Phrygian.

  Attention:
  1) It is very important to emphasize that this concept of substitution chords, can work
  melodically or harmonically. However, be careful when using it harmonically, because the
  melody of the song may not Hit with the new harmony. On the other hand,melodically it will
  work perfectly most of the time, giving our improvisations new life and color.

  2) While building our lines it is important to emphasize that we should not use or think
  about scales to apply the "secret of the two chords". Think about “pure” major 7th and
  minor 7th melodic lines.

  3) Another important thing to understand is that we do not have to use the complete major
  7th or minor 7th chords and arpeggios. We can simply use triads, as we will see in some
                               68


  examples on the following pages.
                        46




  Summarizing :

  Over C#7alt you can play lines from → Cmaj7 & Am7
                                        Fmaj7 & Dm7
                                        Bbmaj7 & Gm7

  On the f ollowing pages, we have some examples of major 7th and minor 7th ideas used
  over dominant altered chords. All the examples were taken from recordings as indicated.
  Enjoy the examples below:
